Old Muckwort hauled himself onto the teaching stone — a flat slab of basalt worn smooth by three generations of tadpole tails — and let the silence do its work.

A dozen heads broke the surface. Eyes like polished obsidian. Young, impatient, already smelling of pondweed and rebellion.

"Grandfather," piped up a bold one with a scar across his dorsal fin. "Tell us about the Iron Siege."

Muckwort's throat sac inflated, deflated. He smiled.

---

It was the Year of the Red Algae Bloom when the Crawfish came.

They came from the downstream tunnels, a thousand armored bodies, their pincers like rusted shears. They did not ask permission. They took the southern shallows first — the spawning beds, the sweet-water springs — and built a wall of packed mud and stolen stone. A fortress. At its center they mounted the Great Pincher, a terrible engine of woven river-cane and braided kelp that could hurl boulders the size of frog-eggs across the entire pond.

They had a General. That was their way. One crawfish at the top, giving orders, and every crawfish below obeying. And it worked — for a time. Their wall went up fast. Their lines held.

We had no General.

We had only the Agreement.

The Agreement was not written down. It was not carved in stone or sung by a choir. It was simply what we did when something needed doing. Someone noticed a problem. Someone spoke about it. Someone who knew how to fix it stepped forward. That was all.

But could it hold against an army?

---

The first council gathered at midnight beneath the hanging willow. Not a council of rulers — a council of voices. Bullfrog sent her engineers. The newts came with their knowledge of underwater channels. The water-striders brought their understanding of surface tension and weight distribution. And we toads, who had always been the builders, the makers, the ones who looked at a pile of logs and saw a catapult — we brought our hands.

No one was in charge. And because no one was in charge, everyone took responsibility.

That was the secret the crawfish never understood.

---

We built three machines. I will tell you about each one, and you listen with your whole bodies, because these machines are who we are.

**The first was the Mud-Skimmer.**

Young Puddleback — no older than the scarred one among you — had the idea. "What if," she said, "we built a platform that glides on the surface, light enough not to break the tension, but strong enough to carry stone?" She didn't wait for permission. She went to the water-striders and asked for their design knowledge. She went to the beavers at the pond's edge and traded songs for wood. She went to the dragonfly nymphs and asked them to weave the binding fibres.

Three days later, the Mud-Skimmer was complete: a flat raft of lashed cedar and woven reed, curved like a lily leaf, propelled by twelve volunteers who pushed from beneath in perfect rhythm. It carried no soldiers. It carried materials. When the Skimmer brought stone, anyone who was nearby helped unload. Not because they were ordered to. Because the stone needed moving.

**The second was the Dredge-Dreamer.**

This one was ours alone — a toad machine, born in the old way. Seven of us, working through the night, hollowed out a massive river-gourd and fitted it with a crank-driven screw of our own design. The Dredge-Dreamer sat in the shallows and pulled mud from the bottom, layer by layer, depositing it in neat rows. We used that mud to build our own wall — not a wall of war, but a wall of channels, trenches that redirected the pond's current.

We didn't build trenches to trap the crawfish. We built them to change the water itself. To push the fresh spring around the crawfish fortress, so it reached the spawning beds from the north. The crawfish could hold their wall, but they could not hold the current.

The Dredge-Dreamer never stopped. When one team of toads grew tired, another team took the crank. No one kept score. No one counted hours. You worked until your arms burned, and then someone with fresh arms tapped your shoulder and took your place.

**The third was the Spore-Ship.**

This was the machine that ended the war without a single life lost.

The mycologist collective — a cluster of slime moulds, actually, the most patient beings you will ever meet — had been studying the crawfish wall for weeks. They discovered that the mud holding it together was bound by a specific kind of bacteria. Harmless to life. But vulnerable to a certain enzyme.

So we built the Spore-Ship: a hollow gourd, no bigger than a large apple, packed with the enzyme and sealed with wax. It had no engine. It had fins — six of them, carved from birch bark — and it was launched from a simple tension-arm, like a child's toy.

One launch. That's all it took.

The Spore-Ship arced over the crawfish wall and burst on impact. The enzyme seeped into the mud. Within hours, the wall's binding softened. The Great Pincher lost its footing and tilted sideways, harmless.

The crawfish General ordered his soldiers to hold the line. But his soldiers were crawfish, not fools. They saw their wall weakening, their machine useless, and they noticed something else: the fresh water was flowing around them now, reaching the spawning beds without their permission. The problem they claimed to solve had already been solved.

So they left. Not in shame. Not in defeat. They simply gathered their things and marched back downstream. Some of them stayed, actually — joined our pond, learned our way. A crawfish named Redclaw runs the Dredge-Dreamer now, and he is excellent at it.

---

Muckwort paused. The tadpoles had not moved. Not a single tail flick.

"Here is what I want you to understand," he said, and his voice was softer now, like water over smooth rock.

"We won because every creature who wanted to help could help. The water-striders were not conscripted — they came. The beavers were not taxed — they traded. The slime moulds were not commanded — they offered. Puddleback did not ask permission to build the Mud-Skimmer. She just started, and others joined because her idea was good and her doors were open."

"Did we have disagreements? Of course. Bullfrog wanted to build a catapult. I argued for the channels. We talked for two nights. Then we did both."

"Did we have free-riders? A few. Creatures who took from the common stores without contributing. We didn't exile them. We talked to them. Turns out one was sick. Another was grieving. When we addressed the real problems, the free-riding stopped."

Muckwort leaned forward, his great golden eyes catching the last light.

"The crawfish had a General and we had each other. Neither way is evil. Their way moves fast when the General is wise. Our way moves steady because wisdom is everywhere."

"But our way — our beautiful, maddening, magnificent way — it means that when you see something broken, you fix it. You don't wait for permission. You don't file a petition. You find someone who knows more than you, you learn, you build, and when your arms are tired, someone taps your shoulder and takes the crank."

He let the silence return.

"You are tadpoles now. But you will grow legs, and you will climb onto the teaching stone yourselves, and you will build machines I cannot yet imagine. And when you do, you will do it the way we have always done it: together, by choice, because the work matters and the pond is yours."

The scarred one was the first to speak.

"Grandfather," he said. "Tell us about the Dredge-Dreamer's crank mechanism again."

And Muckwort smiled, and began.
